worksheet.title: Read Both Scripts
worksheet.subtitle: Two moves each — find where both land
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read two scripts that run at the same time and find where each one lands.

parts.title: Two scripts, one green flag
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) each have their OWN script. Now each script has TWO moves. When you press the green flag ▶, BOTH scripts run at the SAME time — that is concurrent. Read one move at a time. Each sprite moves on the number path 0 to 5.

parts.title: Where does Bit land?
parts.prompt: Read Bit's script from 0: forward 3, then back 1. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Where does Pixel land?
parts.prompt: Read Pixel's script from 5: back 2, then forward 1. What number does Pixel land on?

parts.title: Predict — both at once
parts.prompt: The green flag starts BOTH scripts together. Write where EACH sprite lands. Bit: ____  Pixel: ____. Do they land on the same number?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Even when both scripts run at the same time, you read each one move by move. Each sprite follows only its own script, so each one lands on its own number.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Bit and Pixel each have TWO moves now. Students read both sets of moves and find where each character lands when the green flag starts both at the same time. More moves to trace, still two sets running at once. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: put two counters on a number line 0 to 5 — green for Bit, purple for Pixel — and move BOTH at the same time so children see the two sets of moves run side by side.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Read Bit's two moves in order, then Pixel's two moves in order.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit lands on 2; Exercise 2 — Pixel lands on 4.
3. Let them try. Students write where each lands when both start, and whether they meet (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Bit: 0, forward 3 → 3, back 1 → 2. Exercise 2 — Pixel: 5, back 2 → 3, forward 1 → 4.
Exercise 3 — both start on the green flag: Bit lands on 2, Pixel on 4. Different numbers, so they do not meet.
Key idea: each character's moves change only its own position; the green flag starts both together.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: mixing the two characters — doing one of Bit's moves, then one of Pixel's. Finish one character's moves, then the other's.
Make it easier: trace Bit fully with a green counter, then Pixel with a purple counter.
Make it harder: ask who travelled more steps in total.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions, including two sets that run at the same time.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read two sets of instructions, change one, and explain what happens when both run together.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child traces both two-move sets and writes both landing numbers.
